notions.titre: Mass production and the birth of modern advertising
notions.question: Why was modern advertising born in the United States at the end of the 19th century?
notions.definition: After the Civil War, American industrialization made mass production possible, and output came to exceed local demand: manufacturers had to sell growing volumes on a market that had become national thanks to the railroad, the telegraph and the postal service. Advertising then changed function: it no longer simply announced that a product was available; it had to create demand and build consumer loyalty to a brand. This period saw the rise of national packaged brands (branded goods), which replaced anonymous products sold in bulk (Procter & Gamble's Ivory soap, 1879; Coca-Cola, 1886; Uneeda biscuits, 1898), of major national magazines financed by advertising (Ladies' Home Journal, 1883) and of mail-order catalogs (Montgomery Ward, Sears). The excesses of "patent medicines" (miracle cures) contributed to the passage of the Pure Food and Drug Act of 1906. By the early 20th century, advertising had become an industry in its own right, at the heart of American consumer culture.

etapes: Industrialization and mass production: supply exceeds demand
Unification of the national market (railroad, mail, telegraph)
National packaged brands: the manufacturer addresses the consumer directly
National magazine press financed by advertising
Advertising must create demand and brand loyalty

fonctionnement.texte: The key shift is the move from informational advertising (announcement) to persuasive advertising that creates needs and associates the brand with values.

termes.definition: Manufacturing in very large standardized runs.
Name or sign identifying a manufacturer's products.
Standardized product sold in packaging under the manufacturer's brand.
Society in which the consumption of goods is central to social life.

exemple.texte: The campaign launched in 1899 by the N. W. Ayer & Son agency for the National Biscuit Company's Uneeda biscuits, with sealed branded packaging, is often cited as one of the first major national campaigns for an everyday consumer product.

notions.titre: The agencies: Ayer, Lasker, Hopkins and reason-why
notions.question: How did advertising agencies become professionalized between 1870 and 1930?
notions.definition: The first agencies were brokers of advertising space who bought pages from newspapers and resold them to advertisers. N. W. Ayer & Son (Philadelphia, 1869) transformed the business by offering advertisers an "open contract" and a transparent commission, and then the design of the ads themselves: the agency became a service provider for the advertiser. In Chicago, at Lord & Thomas, Albert Lasker adopted John E. Kennedy's formula "salesmanship in print" (advertising is selling in writing) in 1904 and developed "reason-why" copy: a reasoned text that gives readers concrete reasons to buy. Claude Hopkins, a copywriter at Lord & Thomas, systematized this approach in "Scientific Advertising" (1923): measure effectiveness through reply coupons, test ads, prefer precise facts to vague formulas. At the opposite end, the "atmosphere" or impressionistic school (Theodore MacManus, Cadillac ad "The Penalty of Leadership," 1915) relied on image and emotion.

termes.definition: Company that designs and places advertising on behalf of advertisers.
Company that pays for the advertising.
Writer of advertising texts.
The written part of an ad.
Advertising based on concrete arguments.

exemple.texte: Claude Hopkins recounts that he made Schlitz beer sell by describing how the bottles were washed with live steam, a process that was in fact common to all brewers: the first to explain a fact makes it his own in the public's eyes.

confusions.explication: Two rival schools that would later resurface in the opposition between the USP and the creative revolution.

notions.question: How does public relations differ from advertising, and what role did Edward Bernays play?
notions.definition: Public relations seeks to shape opinion about an organization or a cause, often without any visible paid advertising: press releases, events, endorsements relayed by experts and journalists. In 1906 Ivy Lee published a "Declaration of Principles" promising accurate information to the press. Edward L. Bernays (1891-1995), Sigmund Freud's nephew, worked during World War I for the Committee on Public Information (the Creel Committee), which was in charge of American propaganda. He then theorized the profession in "Crystallizing Public Opinion" (1923) and "Propaganda" (1928), where he argued that an enlightened minority must organize the opinion of the masses; he would later speak of the "engineering of consent" (1947). For the American Tobacco Company, in 1929 he arranged for young women smoking cigarettes, presented as "torches of freedom," to appear in the Easter Parade in New York, in order to break the taboo on women smoking. His methods raise ethical questions about the manipulation of opinion.

termes.definition: Management of an organization's image and of its relations with public opinion.
Organized dissemination of ideas to influence opinion.
Bernays's phrase for organizing public support.
Influential person who relays a message.

exemple.texte: In 1929, Bernays had young women march down Fifth Avenue smoking during the Easter Parade, presenting their cigarettes as "torches of freedom"; the stunt, commissioned by the American Tobacco Company, was reported by the press as a gesture of emancipation.

confusions.explication: PR targets opinion through unpaid and often indirect channels.

verification: Why does the "torches of freedom" stunt raise an ethical question?

notions.question: How did American advertising try to measure its audience and its effectiveness?
notions.definition: From the 1920s on, advertisers and agencies wanted to know their audience and check whether their spending was effective. George Gallup, hired by the Young & Rubicam agency in 1932, applied the sample survey (sampling) to ad readership, then founded the American Institute of Public Opinion in 1935; in 1936, his poll based on a representative sample predicted Roosevelt's reelection, whereas the Literary Digest's huge mail survey had forecast his defeat. Arthur C. Nielsen founded his company in 1923 and measured radio and then television audiences (Nielsen ratings) using a device that recorded the stations tuned in (the Audimeter): these measurements set the price of advertising space. In the 1950s, Ernest Dichter's "motivation research" applied psychoanalysis to consumption; Vance Packard denounced it in "The Hidden Persuaders" (1957). Market research now combines quantitative data (polls, ratings) and qualitative data (interviews, groups).

fonctionnement.texte: The size of a sample does not guarantee its reliability: what counts is how representative it is (the lesson of 1936).

termes.definition: Collection and analysis of information about a market and its consumers.
Subgroup that reproduces the characteristics of the population.
Number or share of people exposed to a program.
Survey of the opinions of a sample.

exemple.texte: A fictional television network charges 20% more for a commercial slot in a program whose measured audience has grown by 20%: audience measurement becomes the currency of the advertising market.

confusions.explication: The Digest mainly surveyed well-off households; Gallup, with fewer responses, had a more representative sample.

notions.titre: Television and the Unique Selling Proposition
notions.question: How did television transform American advertising in the 1950s?
notions.definition: Television spread very rapidly through American households: fewer than 10% owned a set in 1950, nearly 90% in 1960. It became the leading medium of postwar mass consumption. At first, a single advertiser sponsored an entire program, which often bore its name (sponsorship); after the quiz show scandals (1958-1959), the networks took back control of programming and sold commercial slots to several advertisers (spots). Rosser Reeves, of the Ted Bates agency, formalized the "Unique Selling Proposition" (USP) in "Reality in Advertising" (1961): each ad must make a specific proposition, one that the competition does not make, and one strong enough to attract new customers, repeated relentlessly (example: M&M's, "melts in your mouth, not in your hand"). In 1952 Reeves also created the "Eisenhower Answers America" spots, marking the entry of television advertising into presidential campaigns.

items: Proposition: a concrete benefit for the consumer
Unique: the competition does not (or cannot) put it forward
Strong: able to make people switch brands
Repetition: the same message, over a long period, at high frequency

The network sells slots to several advertisers

termes.definition: Distinctive benefit highlighted repeatedly.
Short audiovisual advertising message.

exemple.texte: Rosser Reeves's slogan for M&M's, "melts in your mouth, not in your hand," illustrates the USP: a concrete benefit, specific to the product, repeated for years.

confusions.explication: The USP must state a distinctive benefit, not just a catchy phrase.

notions.question: What was the "creative revolution," and how did it break with the advertising of the 1950s?
notions.definition: In the 1960s, a new generation of New York advertising people rejected the hammering repetition of the USP and what they saw as the condescending advertising of the 1950s. Bill Bernbach (Doyle Dane Bernbach agency, DDB, founded in 1949) had copywriters and art directors work together, and relied on humor, apparent honesty and the reader's intelligence. His campaign for Volkswagen ("Think Small," 1959) presented a small German car as a smart choice compared with big American cars; his campaign for Avis ("We try harder," 1962) turned second place into a selling point. David Ogilvy (Ogilvy & Mather) combined elegance, research and brand image (the Hathaway man with the eye patch, 1951; Rolls-Royce, 1958); Leo Burnett, in Chicago, created iconic characters (the Marlboro Man, 1955). According to the historian Thomas Frank, this creative revolution co-opted the codes of the counterculture (nonconformism, irony) in order to sell: "hip consumerism."

Pair made up of a copywriter and an art director.
Making fun of oneself, here of one's own product.
How the brand is represented in the public's mind.

exemple.texte: DDB's "Think Small" ad for the Volkswagen Beetle (1959) shows a tiny car in a large white space with ironic copy: it became the emblem of the creative revolution.

confusions.explication: According to Frank, advertising appropriated the codes of the counterculture rather than being part of it.

notions.titre: Regulating advertising: the FTC and tobacco
notions.question: How does the U.S. federal government regulate advertising, and why is tobacco an emblematic case?
notions.definition: The Federal Trade Commission (FTC), created by the Federal Trade Commission Act of 1914, was initially responsible for unfair competition. The Wheeler-Lea Act of 1938 extended its jurisdiction to "unfair or deceptive acts or practices" toward consumers, which enabled it to prosecute false advertising. The FTC requires claims to be backed up (the "substantiation" doctrine, 1972) and can impose corrective advertising, as with Listerine mouthwash, which was ordered in 1975, and upheld on appeal in 1977, to correct the claim that it prevented colds. Advertising nevertheless enjoys constitutional protection: in 1976 the Supreme Court recognized that "commercial speech" is protected by the First Amendment, subject to limits (Central Hudson decision, 1980). Tobacco illustrates this evolution: after the Surgeon General's report of January 1964 linking smoking and cancer, the Federal Cigarette Labeling and Advertising Act (1965) required a health warning on packs, and then the Public Health Cigarette Smoking Act (1970) banned cigarette advertising on radio and television from January 2, 1971. The Master Settlement Agreement of November 1998 between the major cigarette makers and 46 states further restricted advertising (billboards, cartoon characters targeting young people).

Further restrictions, targeting of young people banned

fonctionnement.texte: In the United States, regulation combines federal law, FTC action, state litigation and self-regulation by the industry (National Advertising Division, 1971); First Amendment protection limits blanket bans.

notions.question: Why did American advertising move from the mass market to segments?
notions.definition: In a 1956 article, Wendell R. Smith contrasted two strategies: product differentiation, which seeks to attract the whole market, and market segmentation, which adapts the offering to groups of consumers with distinct needs. From the 1950s-1960s on, American advertising increasingly targeted segments: young people ("Pepsi Generation," 1963), working women, the African American and then the Hispanic market, categories defined by lifestyle (the VALS typology, Values and Lifestyles, 1978). The historian Lizabeth Cohen shows that this segmentation fragmented the postwar "consumers' republic" into separate markets. Cable (MTV, 1981) and specialized media made this targeting easier, and digital media later pushed it down to the individual level.

Segment targeted by a campaign.
Market treated as an undifferentiated whole.
Communication targeting a cultural community.

exemple.texte: In "A Consumers' Republic" (2003), Lizabeth Cohen describes the shift, from the 1960s on, from a unified mass market to markets segmented by age, gender, ethnic origin and lifestyle.

confusions.explication: The distinction drawn by Wendell Smith (1956).

notions.question: How has digital technology transformed American advertising?
notions.definition: The first banner ad is generally dated to October 1994, on the HotWired website (an AT&T ad). In 2000 Google launched its AdWords program: the advertiser pays per click (pay-per-click) and targets according to the keywords searched. Social networks (Facebook advertising from 2007) allow targeting based on the user's profile, interests and behavior, tracked through cookies and trackers; programmatic advertising buys space automatically through real-time auctions. Influencer marketing turns content creators into advertising relays; the FTC requires paid partnerships to be disclosed (Endorsement Guides). This model, which Shoshana Zuboff calls "surveillance capitalism," raises privacy issues (Cambridge Analytica scandal, 2018). In the United States, there is no general federal data protection law comparable to the European GDPR; sector-specific laws (COPPA, 1998, for children under 13) and state laws (California) regulate data collection.

Targeted display, measurement of clicks and conversions

fonctionnement.texte: Payment per click (CPC) or per thousand impressions (CPM): digital advertising allows fine-grained measurement, but also click fraud and dependence on a handful of platforms.

notions.question: How do you analyze an advertisement as a cultural and historical document?
notions.definition: Analyzing an advertisement means describing its components, explaining its persuasive techniques and placing it in its historical and cultural context. First, identify the advertiser, the brand, the medium, the date and the presumed target. Then describe the composition: headline, body copy, visual, tagline (slogan), logo, call to action. Roland Barthes (« Rhétorique de l'image », 1964) distinguishes the denoted message (what is literally seen) from the connoted message (the associated cultural meanings). Analyze the levers of persuasion: rational argument (logos), credibility of the source (ethos), emotion (pathos); the AIDA model (attention, interest, desire, action) sums up the intended path. Finally, interpret what the ad reveals about society: gender roles, ethnic representations, values (freedom, success, family), and assess what it leaves out.

Describe: composition, headline, copy, visual, slogan, logo

reponse.corrige: Ad A relies on abundance and status: the headline "Bigger, Better, Bolder" and the chrome-laden sedan connote postwar prosperity and suburban family success, while the body copy piles up claims about power and size, in the insistent style of 1950s advertising. Ad B, by contrast, adopts the self-deprecating tone of the creative revolution: its headline admits a weakness, the white space isolates the small car, and the ironic copy treats readers as intelligent consumers who value thrift over display. Whereas A targets the desire for social recognition, B flatters the reader's sense of being smarter than the conformist crowd.

synthese.titre: American civilization: advertising and marketing, the essentials
synthese.essentiel: Modern advertising was born in the United States after the Civil War: mass production and a national market forced manufacturers to create demand and brand loyalty. It then professionalized (agencies, reason-why, PR), learned to measure itself (Gallup, Nielsen), boomed with television (USP, creative revolution), was regulated (FTC, tobacco) and fragmented into segments and digital targeting. Know dates, names, campaigns; analyze ads in context.

chapitres.memo: Gallup counts opinions, Nielsen counts TV sets, Dichter digs into the unconscious, Packard blows the whistle.

questions.q: Why did Gallup beat the Literary Digest in 1936?
questions.r: His sample, though smaller, was representative; the Digest surveyed mainly well-off households.

questions.q: What did Nielsen measure and why did it matter?
questions.r: Radio then TV audiences (Audimeter); ratings set the price of advertising space.

questions.q: Match Dichter and Packard.
questions.r: Dichter: motivation research (1950s); Packard: its critique in 'The Hidden Persuaders' (1957).

chapitres.idee: Television made advertising the engine of postwar mass consumption: first the repeated USP of the 1950s, then the witty, ironic creative revolution of the 1960s.
points: TV in households: under 10% in 1950, nearly 90% in 1960
Sponsorship (one advertiser controls a program) → spots sold by networks after the quiz show scandals (1958-1959)
USP (Rosser Reeves, Ted Bates): a concrete proposition, unique, strong enough to make people switch, repeated (M&M's)
Bernbach (DDB, 1949): copywriter + art director team, humor, apparent honesty, reader's intelligence
DDB: Volkswagen 'Think Small' (1959), Avis 'We try harder' (1962)
Ogilvy: brand image (Hathaway man, 1951; Rolls-Royce, 1958); Leo Burnett: Marlboro Man (1955)
Thomas Frank: 'hip consumerism', ads co-opt counterculture codes (nonconformism, irony)

dates.fait: Reeves's 'Eisenhower Answers America' spots: TV ads enter presidential campaigns
Quiz show scandals: end of sponsorship, rise of spots
VW 'Think Small' (DDB)
Reeves, 'Reality in Advertising' formalizes the USP
Avis 'We try harder'

distinctions.a: 1950s USP: serious, repetitive; reader convinced by repetition
distinctions.b: Creative revolution: humor, irony; reader intelligent and complicit
distinctions.difference: Opposite tone and organization (separate copywriter and designer vs creative team).
The USP must state a distinctive benefit, not just a catchy phrase.
For Frank, advertising appropriated counterculture codes rather than being part of it.

chapitres.memo: M&M's melts in your mouth (one message, hammered) vs the tiny Beetle in a sea of white space (a wink).

questions.q: What are the components of the USP?
questions.r: A concrete proposition, unique to the brand, strong enough to win new customers, repeated relentlessly (Reeves, 1961).

questions.q: Why did networks switch from sponsorship to spots?
questions.r: The rigged quiz show scandals (1958-1959) discredited advertisers' control of programs.

questions.q: Name two DDB campaigns with dates.
questions.r: Volkswagen 'Think Small' (1959) and Avis 'We try harder' (1962).

questions.q: What is 'hip consumerism'?
questions.r: Thomas Frank: consumption presented as nonconformist and rebellious, co-opting counterculture codes.

chapitres.idee: US advertising is regulated by the FTC against deceptive practices but protected as commercial speech by the First Amendment; tobacco shows the step-by-step tightening.
points: FTC created in 1914 for unfair competition; Wheeler-Lea Act (1938) adds deceptive practices toward consumers
FTC tools: substantiation of claims (1972), corrective advertising (Listerine, 1975, upheld 1977)
Commercial speech protected by the First Amendment (1976), with limits (Central Hudson, 1980)
Tobacco: Surgeon General (Jan. 1964), pack warning (1965), radio/TV ban (1970 law, effective Jan. 2, 1971), MSA (1998)
MSA with 46 states: billboards and cartoon characters targeting the young restricted
Regulation = federal law + FTC + state litigation + self-regulation (NAD, 1971)

dates.fait: Federal Trade Commission Act: FTC created
Wheeler-Lea Act: unfair or deceptive acts toward consumers
Surgeon General's report links smoking and cancer
Cigarette Labeling and Advertising Act: warning on packs
Cigarette ads banned on radio and TV (Public Health Cigarette Smoking Act, 1970)
Supreme Court: commercial speech protected / Central Hudson limits
Master Settlement Agreement (November, 46 states)

distinctions.difference: The FTC is the general authority on deceptive advertising.
Print and billboards stayed legal, then were restricted in 1998.

chapitres.memo: Tobacco ladder 64-65-71-98: report, warning, off the air, settlement.

questions.q: What did the Wheeler-Lea Act (1938) change?
questions.r: It extended FTC jurisdiction to unfair or deceptive acts toward consumers, allowing it to prosecute false advertising.

questions.q: Since when are cigarette ads banned on US radio and TV?
questions.r: January 2, 1971 (Public Health Cigarette Smoking Act, 1970).

questions.q: Does US advertising enjoy constitutional protection?
questions.r: Yes: commercial speech is protected by the First Amendment (1976), within limits (Central Hudson, 1980).

questions.q: What is corrective advertising? Give the example.
questions.r: An FTC order to correct a false claim: Listerine (1975, upheld 1977) had to correct that it prevented colds.

chapitres.idee: The mass market split into segments from the 1950s-1960s, and digital media pushed targeting down to the individual through personal data, raising privacy issues.
points: Wendell R. Smith (1956): product differentiation vs market segmentation
Segments: young people (Pepsi Generation, 1963), working women, African American then Hispanic markets, lifestyles (VALS, 1978)
Criteria: demographic, geographic, psychographic (values, lifestyle), behavioral (frequency, loyalty)
Lizabeth Cohen, 'A Consumers' Republic' (2003): segmentation fragments the postwar mass market; cable (MTV, 1981)
Digital: banner (Oct. 1994, HotWired, AT&T), Google AdWords pay-per-click (2000), Facebook ads (2007), programmatic real-time auctions
Influencers: FTC requires disclosure of paid partnerships (Endorsement Guides)
Zuboff: 'surveillance capitalism'; Cambridge Analytica (2018); no US equivalent of GDPR, only COPPA (1998, under 13) and state laws (California)
formules: CPC = cost per click; CPM = cost per thousand impressions

distinctions.b: Market segmentation (adapt offer to distinct groups)

distinctions.difference: The cookie collects; the legal issue is the data.
The US has no general federal data protection law.

chapitres.memo: From one mass to many slices (Smith, Cohen) to one person per screen (cookies, Zuboff).

questions.q: Targeting by values and lifestyle is which type of segmentation?
questions.r: Psychographic (e.g. VALS, 1978).

questions.q: Give four landmarks of US digital advertising.
questions.r: First banner (1994, HotWired), AdWords pay-per-click (2000), Facebook advertising (2007), Cambridge Analytica scandal (2018).

questions.q: 10,000 clicks, 300 purchases: conversion rate?
How is personal data protected in the US?
questions.r: No general federal law like GDPR: sector laws (COPPA 1998, children under 13) and state laws (California); FTC disclosure rules.

chapitres.idee: Analyzing an ad means identifying it, describing it, decoding denotation and connotation, explaining its persuasion and interpreting it in its historical context.
points: Identify: advertiser, brand, product, medium, date, presumed target
Describe: headline, body copy, visual, tagline/slogan, logo, call to action
Barthes ('Rhétorique de l'image', 1964): denoted message (what is seen) vs connoted message (cultural meanings); Panzani 'Italianicity'
Persuasion: logos (argument), ethos (credibility), pathos (emotion); AIDA path
Context: period and school (reason-why, USP, creative revolution)
Critical interpretation: gender roles, ethnic representations, values, stereotypes, omissions

distinctions.difference: Without a source, speak of a presumed target.
'A smiling woman in a kitchen' is denotation; 'modernity, prosperity' is connotation.

chapitres.memo: I-D-D-C-P-C-I: Identify, Describe, Denote, Connote, Persuade, Context, Interpret.

questions.q: What is the English term for the argumentative text of an ad?
questions.r: Body copy.

questions.q: What are Barthes's two levels of the image?
questions.r: Denoted message (literal) and connoted message (cultural associations), e.g. Panzani's 'Italianicity'.

questions.q: 1950s fridge ad, 'Give her the kitchen she deserves': what to note?
questions.r: Presumed target the husband; gendered division of roles; the fridge connotes modernity and postwar prosperity.

parCoeur: N. W. Ayer & Son 1869; 'salesmanship in print' 1904; Hopkins 'Scientific Advertising' 1923
Brands: Ivory 1879, Coca-Cola 1886, Uneeda 1898; Pure Food and Drug Act 1906
Nielsen 1923; Gallup at Y&R 1932, AIPO 1935, correct forecast 1936; Packard 1957
TV households: under 10% (1950) → about 90% (1960); quiz show scandals 1958-1959
USP: Rosser Reeves, Ted Bates, 'Reality in Advertising' 1961, M&M's
DDB: VW 'Think Small' 1959, Avis 'We try harder' 1962; Marlboro Man 1955
FTC 1914; Wheeler-Lea 1938; commercial speech 1976; Central Hudson 1980
Tobacco: 1964 report, 1965 warning, Jan. 2, 1971 radio/TV ban, 1998 MSA
Wendell Smith 1956; Pepsi Generation 1963; VALS 1978; MTV 1981
Digital: banner 1994, AdWords 2000, Facebook ads 2007, Cambridge Analytica 2018; COPPA 1998
pieges: Believing all tobacco advertising was banned in 1971: only radio and TV
Thinking a bigger sample is more reliable: representativeness is what counts (1936)
Confusing PR (opinion, indirect, unpaid channels) with advertising (paid space)
Saying US advertising has no constitutional protection: commercial speech is protected, within limits
Treating the USP as any catchy slogan, or the creative revolution as part of the counterculture
Stopping at description in an ad analysis, or calling the presumed target the actual target
